reference.source: ERS/ATS guidance and standard respiratory genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Suspect in a child or adult with a lifelong daily wet (productive) cough, recurrent chest and sinus infections, and persistent rhinitis
Around half of patients have situs inversus (Kartagener phenotype), and laterality defects or congenital heart disease raise suspicion
Unexplained neonatal respiratory distress in a term baby, often needing oxygen for days, is an important early clue
Nasal nitric oxide is characteristically very low and is a useful screening tool in cooperative children and adults

Diagnosis rests on a combination of clinical phenotype, low nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat, transmission electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure, and genetic testing
Bronchiectasis develops progressively and tends to affect the middle and lower lobes, unlike the upper-lobe predominance often seen in cystic fibrosis
Male infertility (immotile sperm) and reduced female fertility are common because motile cilia and flagella share structural components
Management is largely supportive with airway clearance, prompt antibiotic treatment of infective exacerbations, and surveillance of lung function and hearing
reference.pathophysiology: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a mostly autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding components of the motile cilium (for example the outer and inner dynein arms and radial spokes). Defective assembly or function of these structures impairs the coordinated beating of respiratory cilia, so mucociliary clearance fails and mucus and bacteria are retained throughout the airways and sinuses. The same defect in embryonic nodal cilia disrupts left-right patterning during development, explaining the frequent situs anomalies, while shared axonemal components account for impaired sperm and fallopian tube function.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable and other primary immunodeficiencies
Chronic aspiration or recurrent viral respiratory infection
Secondary (acquired) ciliary dysfunction from chronic infection or smoke exposure
Foreign body or structural airway anomaly
additionalInvestigations: Nasal nitric oxide measurement as a screening test
High-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat frequency and pattern from a nasal brushing
Transmission electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure
Extended genetic panel for known PCD genes
High-resolution chest imaging to assess for and monitor bronchiectasis
Sputum microbiology and lung function testing
Audiometry and ENT assessment for chronic otitis media with effusion
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness or falling lung function suggesting advancing bronchiectasis
Recurrent isolation of Pseudomonas or non-tuberculous mycobacteria
Situs and cardiac anomalies requiring cardiology assessment in infancy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and structured airway clearance many patients maintain reasonable lung function into adulthood, but chronic infection can cause progressive bronchiectasis, and outcomes vary with genotype, adherence to therapy, and access to specialist multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Attributing lifelong wet cough to recurrent viral infection or asthma and delaying diagnosis for years
Relying on a single test result, as ultrastructure can appear normal in some genetic subtypes
Interpreting nasal nitric oxide as diagnostic in isolation, since it can be low in cystic fibrosis and unreliable during acute infection
Overlooking the situs inversus clue on a chest radiograph
Forgetting to counsel about fertility implications
references: European Respiratory Society statement on primary ciliary dyskinesia
Standard paediatric and adult respiratory medicine texts
management: Institute regular airway clearance physiotherapy to compensate for failed mucociliary clearance
Treat respiratory exacerbations promptly with culture-directed and often prolonged antibiotics
Undertake routine surveillance sputum microbiology and lung-function monitoring
Manage chronic rhinosinusitis and otitis media with nasal saline and steroids, ENT input, and hearing support
Give influenza and pneumococcal immunisations and advise avoidance of tobacco smoke
Monitor progressive bronchiectasis with high-resolution imaging and consider surgery for localised severe disease
Offer genetic counselling for the mostly autosomal recessive inheritance and address subfertility
Coordinate a specialist PCD multidisciplinary team spanning respiratory, ENT, audiology, and fertility services
